context: The success of this report is a result of contribution from various Institutions. The Ministry of Health provided the regulatory and the enabling environment for the implementation of the survey, Makerere University School of Public Health implemented the survey with technical assistance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of Defense (DOD) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). We acknowledge The President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) for funding this survey. Our gratitude goes to the various survey participants from whom these data were collected. We also acknowledge the implementing partners and the district health teams, the Drop-in Centers (DICs), Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and Community Based Organizations (CBOs) that supported the implementation of this survey across the different sites in Uganda.
Executive Summary

This report provides findings from a biobehavioral surveys (BBS) among People Who Inject Drugs (PWID), implemented in 2023 by the Crane Survey Project, a collaborative activity of Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH), Ministry of Health (MoH), the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with funding from the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). The BBS included 5 sites: Gulu, Mbale, Lira, Fort Portal, and Kampala.

The aim of the BBS was to inform HIV programming and policy in Uganda by estimating prevalence of HIV, syphilis, Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and Hepatitis C virus, HIV service uptake (ART coverage, viral load suppression, and CD4 cell count) and HIV prevention services such as Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), risky behaviors (alcohol use, drug use), and depression. The population size of PWID was estimated and the survey employed Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS) design. Main survey findings are summarized in Tables 1-3 below.

context: Initial survey participants (“seeds”) were recruited by the survey team to start enrollment. Seeds were purposively enrolled to reflect a broad array of sociodemographic characteristics (e.g., age, sexual orientation, education, area of residence, marital status, language, religion), HIV status, and affiliation with a HRP organization or HRP service provider. context: 2.2 Laboratory Testing

Laboratory testing was carried out both on-site and off-site. Nearby accredited/certified regional referral hospital laboratories conducted tests for CD4 count and prepared HIV, HBV and HCV viral load samples and provided DBS temporary storage which was later transported to CPHL through the National Hub sample transportation system. Central Public Health Laboratories (CPHL) was responsible for viral load testing and longer DBS storage. Testing using DBS was done at international laboratories at CDC in Atlanta, USA. Material Transfer Agreements (MTA) were signed to enable sample shipment outside Uganda.
2.2.1 Laboratory Procedures

Participants who were eligible and consented had to a maximum of 10 ml of venous blood drawn into EDTA-containing vacutainer tubes. Blood was stored at room temperature or kept at 2-8°C at nearby peripheral hub and later transported to the CPHL where specimens were tested for HIV viral load, HBV and HCV viral load and CD4+ T cell counts. Samples (plasma) were prepared and transported for storage at CPHL at -20°C and -80 °C with consent of participants to allow future testing. Sample storage conditions at CPHL met standard conditions, including daily monitoring of temperature.

context: 2.3 Data Management and Security

A standardized data collection instrument was used to collect data for all survey groups. This instrument was designed in Questionnaire Design Studio (QDS 5.0) with validations, group specific and logical skips and AUDIT functions to measure and automatically score someone according to the risk associated with specific self-reported behavior. The Audio Computer-Assisted Self Interview (ACASI) was the main data collection instrument along with the computer-Assisted Personal Interviews (CAPI), administered by survey staff if needed. Data was collected on characteristics including demographics, HIV-related behavioral risk behaviors, symptoms of STIs, as well as on HIV-related knowledge, attitude, practices, stigma, perceptions, and questions related to mental health or other health-related aspects. Each interview lasted between 45-90 minutes, depending on the participant's responsiveness and speed.
Target Sample Size estimation

For surveys with an HIV prevalence of >10%, the target sample size aimed to estimate VLS with a precision of no more than +/- 10 percentage points. Assuming a design effect of 2 in RDS surveys (Salganik et al., 2006, Salganik et al., 2010), this meant that to collect VL results for about 200 participants (see Table 7 below for varying scenarios). Our total target sample size therefore varied between 500 and 1,700 (larger HIV prevalence required smaller sample sizes). Further we monitored convergence and bottleneck graphs for VLS and HIV prevalence (See Annex 6) and would continue sampling (and introduce new seeds) if convergence had not been reached for both indicators or severe bottlenecks are observed

2.4 Seeds and Enrolment

Seeds were participants who initiated in each referral chain and were purposely selected by the investigators in collaboration with the CBOs. Seed selection prioritized individuals with large social networks, positive community standing, and alignment with survey objectives. To ensure independence and diversity, seeds were chosen from various backgrounds based on age, place of residence, education, socioeconomic status. Seeds met the respective eligibility criteria and were given coupons and instructions for peer recruitment.

Seeds and subsequent participants received 3 coupons at the beginning of the survey and as time progressed, the number of coupons given to recruits per survey site depended on the proportion of coupons redeemed to facilitate continued waves and to enable attainment of the desired sampling size. Due to the varying local contexts of these survey sites that is, the social economic, cultural diversities of these environments, enrolment and participation in some areas required bigger or greater number of seeds to try and capture higher, diverse respondents or create new waves of participants to obtain the sample size and also sustain the survey. 3.1 Population Size Estimates using 3-Source Capture Recapture and Demographic characteristics among PWID Surveyed in 5 Sites, Uganda, 2023

In 2023, the 3SCRC study estimated the population size of PWID across 5 Ugandan cities using both absolute and network-size (SS-PSE) methods. Kampala had the largest estimated number with ~740 (95% CI 580–940). This represented less than 1% of its adult population aged 18+. Generally, the Relative proportions of PWIDs across all the 5 survey study sites were low with all representing less than 1 % of its estimated adult proportions. Overall, results highlight substantial variation in the size and concentration of people who inject drugs across Ugandan cities

3.2 Demographic characteristics of PWID, 2023
rows: This section presents demographic characteristics across 5 districts in Uganda, showing a predominantly young population with the majority under 35 years old. In pooled data (N=805), the weighted median age was 27 years; 33.1% were aged 15–24 years and 41.7% were aged 25–34 years. A number of them had had some level of educational attainment, with 8.7% reporting no schooling and 27.2% had completed secondary school and beyond. A particularly striking finding is the high prevalence of homelessness (68.5%) and an interesting finding showed that (53.5%) were never married. The presence of dependents among most respondents (70.8%), combined with low rates of living with a spouse or partner (20.4%, among those asked), indicates substantial caregiving responsibilities without stable household support.

3.3 Injection drug use behavioral characteristics of PWID, 2023
rows: This section presents characteristics related to injection drug use among the PWIDs. These behaviors include proportion frequency of injection drug use, types of drugs, drug overdose, needle sharing, knowledge of and access to treatment programs. The median age of injection drug initiation was 20 years, with the majority starting between ages 10-19(40.8%) highlighting high injection practices were common among PWID. Majority had injected drug use 1 to 4 times a month (36.2%) in the past six months. 46.7% had shared injection equipment in the six or more months preceding the survey. Most (77.4%) of the had shared needles last 3 times. (69.0%) had knowledge of drug treatment program. An overwhelming (89.0%) wanted to be in drug treatment Program, while just a quarter (26.1%) had ever been on drug treatment Program. Majority had failed to enroll into a drug treatment program in last 12 months. A few (20.8%) had received MAT in last 12 months. Majority (66.2%) had ever attempted to quit IDU in 12 months

3.4 Stigma among PWID participants surveyed in 5 sites of Uganda, 2023
rows: This section highlights that a majority of the PWID were comfortable disclosing their drug use (61%), a substantial proportion experience or anticipate stigma. Around 30% reported having been denied health care due to their injecting drug use in the past 12 months or more, and 58.9% had avoided health care because of fear of stigma. Denial of care and fear of discrimination therefore remain common and likely contribute to delayed or avoided health care utilization among this population. The discomfort with disclosing injection drug use status coupled with the feeling of anticipated stigma encourage self-discrimination tendencies, hence posing significant public health challenges.

3.5 HIV testing history among people who inject drugs (PWID)
rows: Among the PWID who had ever tested for HIV was high, (86.7%). Among the self-reported testing, majority reported a recent negative result (90.5%), while 9.5% reported being HIV-positive. HIV self-testing was moderately utilized, with 42.9% testing within the past 12 months, although nearly one-third had never self-tested. Regarding recency, only about one-third (32.3%) had tested in the last year, while the rest had longer tested intervals, followed by low perceived risk (23.4%) and fear of positive results (12.9%). Most testing occurred in hospitals or clinics (43.8%), with limited use of self-testing (9.5%). Over half of participants did not disclose injecting drug use to providers (52.6%), though most reported respectful treatment (90.1%). Only a small proportion (6.5%) had ever been informed by a healthcare provider that they were HIV-positive.

3.6 HIV, Syphilis, HBV, HCV burdens band HIV viraemia among PWID surveyed in 5 sites of Uganda, 2023
rows: Overall HIV prevalence among was 9.4%, with prevalence increasing markedly with age from 5.0% among those aged 18–24 years to 16.6% among those aged 35+ years. HIV burden was substantially higher among females (26.9%) compared to males (6.2%). Viral load suppression among the PWID living with HIV varied across age groups, highest in the 18–24 years group (78.7%) and lowest among those aged 25–34 years (36.2%), while males (48.4%) had slightly higher suppression rates than females (42.6%). Active syphilis prevalence was relatively low at 3.4%, however, increased with age and was considerably higher among females (10.5%) than males (2.3%). Hepatitis B prevalence was 2.8% increased with age and higher among females (6.7%) than males (2.1%), while hepatitis C prevalence remained very low at 0.7%, with infections observed only among males.

3.7 Reproductive Health Characteristics among PWID
rows: There was relatively low uptake of family planning, with just over one-third of PWID currently using a method (35.7%), whereas most of them not using any (54.4%). Among users, injectable contraceptives were the most common method (57.7%). Most of respondents had ever been pregnant (75.4%), most commonly 1–2 times (57.7%), and the majority reported 1–2 live births (72.9%). Those who had experiences of miscarriage or stillbirth were 40%, those who had received ANC were the majority (66.6%), but stigma within ANC settings was reported by an overwhelming majority (91.7%). HIV testing during pregnancy was common, with over half had tested multiple times during pregnancy (52.7%), and most tested HIV-negative (87.2%). While breastfeeding, HIV testing remained frequent, with all tested respondents reported as HIV-negative. Most respondents had 1–2 living children (66.9%), with the majority of mothers lived with their children (82.5%), and almost all female PWID (99.0%) respondents with children having only 1–2 under-five children.

rows: HIV prevalence by socio-demographic and other characteristics Summary

The study findings reported an overall prevalence among PWID of 9.4%. 3.10 TB Screening by HIV Status
rows: Finding highlight gaps in tuberculosis (TB) screening and communication among individuals who tested HIV positive. However, among the few respondents who were diagnosed with TB (N = 6), all (100%) reported receiving treatment.

3.11 ART Characteristics
rows: Close to two-thirds of respondents (66.4%) were currently on ART, with most receiving services from hospitals or clinics (50.8%), followed by NGOs (23.4%). 3.13 Viral Load and CD4 Count among PWID tested HIV positive
rows: Viral Load and CD4 Count summary

Participants with CD4 counts measured, median CD4 was 493 cells/µL, with over half (56.5%) in Stage 1 (≥500), 18.5% in Stage 2 (350–499), 15.0% in Stage 3 (200–349), and 9.9% in Stage 4 (<200). Median VL count was 74.2 copies/mL, with (39.0%) of the participants having VL count <50, 15.1% for 50–199, 5.2% VL count for 200–999, and 40.6% >999 copies/mL. 44.6% understood their result, and 63.1% preferred receiving results directly from a healthcare worker. Among 36 self-reported HIV-positive participants, 27.0% were aware of the U=U message, and 61.2% believed it to be true.

3.14 Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) Use among HIV negative PWIDs
rows: This section on PrEP shows that among 745 HIV negative PWID, just over half (57.6%) were aware of PrEP, while 24.4% had not heard of it. of those aware, about half (49.8%) had ever been offered PrEP, and almost two-thirds (65.5%) knew where to get PrEP. 59.4% expressed a desire to use PrEP, 14.1% did not want it, 8.6% were unsure. Regarding usage history among those aware, 22.1% had used PrEP in the last 7 days, 11.2% in the past 6 months, 10.8% more than 6 months ago, and 55.8% had never used it. The main reasons for not using PrEP in the last 6 months included lack of knowledge about PrEP (21.4%) or access (22.1%), fear of side effects (17.6%), concern about stigma (13.8%), not feeling the need (10.6%), cost (4.4%), and other reasons (10.1%).
